summary: Cricothyroid muscle related-to External laryngeal nerve injury
detail: An external laryngeal nerve lesion paralyses the cricothyroid, with loss of its tightening effect on the vocal cords.

summary: Cricothyroid ligament: Intrinsic ligament of the larynx, part of the fibroelastic inner tube, described as stretched between the thyroid cartilage and the vocal process, where it forms the vocal ligament. With the cricoid it surrounds the infraglottic cavity.
detail: medically-doubtful: The definition says the cricothyroid ligament is stretched between the thyroid cartilage and the vocal process. Standard teaching: the cricothyroid ligament (conus elasticus) rises from the upper border of the cricoid; only its free upper margin, between the thyroid angle and the vocal process, is the vocal ligament, and its median part joins cricoid arch to thyroid cartilage. The packet itself gives the cricoid-to-thyroid version elsewhere. The result mentions this only in notes; it is not under conflicts, so nothing is listed in affects.

summary: Heimlich manoeuvre: A procedure the lecture describes step by step and card l33 asks for ('how is it relieved'). Folded into the laryngeal obstruction definition; left out because of the limit.

Respiratory and cardiovascular centres: Directly tested by q:3fuxbc, card b24 and the professor's review question 5, but only mentioned inside the Medulla oblongata definition. Consequence of the 50-concept limit (the result's notes say so).

Cricotracheal ligament: Card g8 asks directly what connects the trachea to the larynx, and card l15 lists it; it has its own defining sentence. Only mentioned inside the trachea definition; left out because of the limit.

The packet describes the respiratory-type laryngeal epithelium as 'cylindric stratified'. Standard teaching names respiratory epithelium pseudostratified ciliated columnar, which is the wording one of the packet's own question options uses for the rest of the larynx.
detail: differs-from-standard-teaching; holds 1 item(s): concept:laryngeal-mucosa

evidence.quote: The epithelium is respiratory type (cylindric stratified) throughout
Ciliated pseudostratified columnar type — Lines the rest of the larynx

summary: Foramen of Luschka: The lateral aperture of the fourth ventricle, defined on slide 15 and named in exam:9, hy:7 and cards b12 and b20; only mentioned inside other definitions. Consequence of the 50-concept limit.

The packet says the posterior laryngeal vein drains to the inferior thyroid vein and then the subclavian vein. Standard teaching is that the inferior thyroid veins drain into the brachiocephalic veins.
detail: differs-from-standard-teaching

evidence.quote: Posterior laryngeal vein to the inferior thyroid vein, then the subclavian vein

summary: Vestibular fold (false vocal cord, ventricular band): The boundary that defines both the vestibule and the ventricle; tested by the spaces question and card l23. Listed in the result's notes as left out because of the 50-concept limit.

evidence.quote: Recurrent laryngeal nerve, often damaged accidentally during partial thyroidectomy

summary: Basilar groove: q:hcwy9m asks directly what lies in it and slide 13 gives it a defining sentence; only mentioned inside the Pons and Basilar artery definitions. Consequence of the 50-concept limit.

Cadaveric position of the vocal cords: Position in which the vocal cords are further abducted and fixed because all the intrinsic muscles are paralysed, seen when both the recurrent and the external laryngeal nerves are damaged on both sides.

evidence.quote: If both recurrent and external laryngeal nerves are damaged on both sides, all the intrinsic muscles are paralysed and the cords are further abducted and fixed: the cadaveric position

summary: Slides 15 and 17 carry the heading 'DESCRIPTIVE ANATOMY: THE MIDBRAIN' but describe the floor of the fourth ventricle (pons and medulla) and the nerves emerging from the medulla; the summary places this content under the pons and medulla.

evidence.quote: DESCRIPTIVE ANATOMY: THE MIDBRAIN Posterior Surface The floor of the fourth ventricle is composed of the dorsal surface of the pons and the medulla.

summary: Cerebral peduncle: wrong-alias
detail: The alias 'crus cerebri' is the standard name of a different thing: the anterior part of the cerebral peduncle only (the peduncle also includes the substantia nigra and tegmentum). The result's own notes admit this, yet it is listed as an alias and not reported under conflicts as the instructions require.

summary: Accessory nerve: Cranial nerve XI, one of the mixed nerves; its cranial part emerges from the sulcus behind the olive of the medulla, below the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.
detail: medically-doubtful: The definition calls cranial nerve XI 'one of the mixed nerves', which the packet does say (it groups IX, X and XI as 'the mixed nerves'). Standard teaching is that the accessory nerve is purely motor; only IX and X of that group are mixed. The result does not report this under conflicts, so nothing lists concept:accessory-nerve as affected.

summary: The packet names the thickenings of the thyrohyoid membrane the medial thyroid ligament and lateral thyroid ligaments. The standard names are the median thyrohyoid ligament and the lateral thyrohyoid ligaments.
detail: differs-from-standard-teaching

evidence.quote: with a medial thickening (medial thyroid ligament) and two lateral thickenings (lateral thyroid ligaments)

summary: Vocal nodule: Inflammatory nodule that develops in people who overuse the voice, at the junction of the anterior one third and posterior two thirds of the vocal cords, the area of maximum contact during vibration. Nodules are bilateral and symmetrical, soft and reddish early, later greyish or whitish.

evidence.quote: Vocal nodules form at the junction of the anterior third and posterior two thirds of the cords

summary: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury: Damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, often accidental during partial thyroidectomy. Unilaterally, the cord on the affected side lies in the paramedian position and does not vibrate, though the other usually compensates; bilaterally, both cords lie paramedian with loss of phonation and difficulty breathing.

evidence.quote: Recurrent laryngeal nerve, often damaged accidentally during partial thyroidectomy: unilaterally, the cord lies in the paramedian position and does not vibrate, though the other usually compensates

summary: Medullary velum (superior and inferior): Forms the roof of the fourth ventricle, with a defining sentence on slide 29; needed for q:1ll2t2d and card b20. Only mentioned inside the Fourth ventricle definition. Consequence of the 50-concept limit.
Anteroinferior laryngeal artery: Has its own table row and slide bullet and is part of card l28 on the arterial supply; the other two laryngeal arteries have concepts. Left out because of the limit.

Interpeduncular fossa: The landmark where CN III leaves, given a defining sentence on slide 11 and used in the answers to q:bapl3l and q:rm6xhf and in card b8; only mentioned inside other definitions. Consequence of the 50-concept limit.

The packet says the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve perforates the cricothyroid membrane and gives sensory innervation to the subglottic stage. Standard teaching is that the external laryngeal nerve is motor to the cricothyroid and that sensation below the vocal folds comes from the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which the packet also states elsewhere.
detail: differs-from-standard-teaching; holds 1 item(s): concept:external-laryngeal-nerve

evidence.quote: Innervates the cricothyroid muscle and perforates the cricothyroid membrane; sensory innervation of the subglottic stage
Recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles except the cricothyroid, and sensation below the cords

summary: Foramen magnum: The lower connection of the brainstem, one of the three answers to card b4 (the other two are concepts) and a distractor in q:njirnb and q:e3mp4l; not mentioned in any definition. Consequence of the 50-concept limit.
Vestibular ligament: One of the two intrinsic ligaments card l16 asks for, with its own defining sentence. Left out because of the limit.

Slide 20 says the trochlear nerve (CN IV) innervates the 'major oblique muscle' and 'ensures upward gaze'. Standard teaching is that the trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique muscle, which depresses (and intorts) the eye, i.e. downward gaze.
detail: differs-from-standard-teaching

evidence.quote: Nerve IV (pathetic nerve: the only one that emerges on the posterior surface of the brainstem innervates the major oblique muscle of the eye: ensures upward gaze)

summary: The packet lists the cephalic flexure and the mesencephalic (cranial) flexure as two separate bends, and slide 4 places the cephalic flexure between brainstem and spinal cord. In standard teaching the cephalic flexure is the mesencephalic flexure (in the midbrain region), and the bend between hindbrain and spinal cord is the cervical flexure.
detail: differs-from-standard-teaching

evidence.quote: the cephalic flexure: brainstem and spinal cord.
The growing neural tube bends at the cephalic flexure and the mesencephalic (cranial) flexure.

summary: Venous drainage of the larynx: Has its own table row and is half of card l29; no concept covers the laryngeal veins. Left out because of the limit.

The packet says all the intrinsic muscles adduct the vocal cords except the posterior cricoarytenoids, but elsewhere says the cricothyroid tenses the cords rather than adducting them and that the thyroarytenoid relaxes them.
detail: internal

evidence.quote: All of them adduct the vocal cords except the posterior cricoarytenoids, which abduct them
The cricothyroid tenses the cords rather than adducting them

summary: Spinocerebellar tract: Has its own table row and is the unconscious ascending tract a student must tell apart from the conscious ones in q:u2xf18 and card b19; it is not mentioned in any definition. Consequence of the 50-concept limit.

Muscular process of the arytenoid: Needed to answer q:1a0xswg (two distractors insert on it) and cards l11 and l21; the lecture gives it a defining sentence. The vocal process has a concept, this does not. Left out because of the limit.

The packet lists the three acoustic parameters as frequency, intensity and pitch, with pitch depending especially on the shape of the supralaryngeal cavities. In standard teaching the parameter shaped by the resonating cavities is timbre (quality), while pitch is set by the frequency of vocal fold vibration, which the packet itself says elsewhere.
detail: differs-from-standard-teaching; holds 1 item(s): concept:acoustic-parameters-of-the-voice

evidence.quote: pitch, depending on the accommodation of the vocal folds but especially on the shape of the supralaryngeal cavities
pitch depends upon the frequency with which the vocal folds vibrate

summary: Middle cerebellar peduncle: The cerebellar peduncle that connects the pons with the cerebellum; the largest of the three.
detail: evidence-does-not-support: The definition says the middle peduncle is 'the largest of the three', resting only on the parenthesis in hy:4, which follows the word 'pons' and may equally mean that the pons is the largest part, as hy:1 says with the same wording. No other block says the middle peduncle is the largest.

summary: Inferior quadrigeminal brachium: Has its own defining sentence beside the superior brachium (which is a concept) and is needed for q:1ej7qkw and card b7; only mentioned inside the Inferior colliculus definition. Consequence of the 50-concept limit.

Thyroarytenoid muscle: Intrinsic muscle of the larynx that relaxes the vocal cords. The lecture lists a superior part, from the reentrant angle of the thyroid cartilage to the lower third of the arytenoid, and an inferior part among the constrictors of the glottis.
detail: unsupported: The definition makes the superior and inferior thyroarytenoid 'parts' of the one thyroarytenoid muscle that relaxes the cords. The packet lists them as two separate constrictors and never says they are parts of the 'Thyroarytenoid' of the action table; the inferior one is the vocal muscle, which the packet says tenses the cord (and which the result itself gives as an alias of the vocalis concept). Neither evidence quote states the parts.

summary: Foramen of Magendie: The median aperture of the fourth ventricle, a distractor explained in q:11sf1cy and part of card b20 and hy:7; only mentioned inside the Fourth ventricle definition. Consequence of the 50-concept limit.

Alternating syndrome: The association of a peripheral cranial nerve palsy on one side with a hemiplegia on the opposite side. It locates the lesion to a level in the brainstem, the cranial nerve involved indicating the level.

evidence.quote: A peripheral cranial nerve lesion on one side with a hemiplegia on the other locates the lesion to a level in the brainstem.

summary: Alternating syndrome depends-on Pyramidal decussation
detail: The syndrome is crossed because corticospinal fibres passing the cranial nerve have not yet crossed, doing so in the lower medulla.

evidence.quote: the corticospinal fibres running past it have not yet crossed, doing so in the lower medulla

summary: Slide 20 calls cranial nerve XI 'the spinal nerve', while slide 17 calls it the accessory nerve. The standard name is accessory nerve; 'spinal nerve' is the standard name of the nerves arising from the spinal cord, so it was not listed as an alias.
detail: differs-from-standard-teaching

cranial part of accessory(11th)

summary: Acoustic neuroma: The only clinical condition besides the alternating syndrome; it has a high-yield point and its own 'deeper' heading with its presentation, but no concept and no presents-with relations. Not tested by a question or flashcard; left out under the 50-concept limit (the result's notes say so).

Laryngeal obstruction: Blockage of the larynx by a foreign body, causing choking when the explosive cough reflex set off by the very sensitive mucosa of the superior larynx is slowed or absent. The Heimlich manoeuvre of upward and backward abdominal thrusts is used to dislodge the foreign body.

evidence.quote: The mucosa of the superior larynx is very sensitive, so a foreign body causes immediate explosive coughing. If that reflex is slowed or absent, choking follows

detail: Damage to the external laryngeal nerve gives weakness of phonation.

evidence.quote: External laryngeal nerve: weakness of phonation from loss of the tightening effect of the cricothyroid

summary: Supraglottic compartment: Has its own table row and card l23 asks to describe it; the glottic and infraglottic compartments have concepts. Left out because of the limit.
Transverse fissure of Bichat connects Brainstem
detail: medically-doubtful: The packet supports 'the brainstem connects above to the diencephalon by the transverse fissure of Bichat', but in standard teaching the transverse cerebral fissure (of Bichat) is a cleft separating the cerebral hemispheres from the diencephalon and brainstem; it does not join the midbrain to the diencephalon, which are directly continuous. A fissure is also not a connecting structure, and the packet's own question says it 'separates'. Not reported under conflicts.

summary: Transverse fissure of Bichat: The fissure at the upper limit of the brainstem, by which the brainstem connects above with the diencephalon.
detail: medically-doubtful: The packet supports 'the brainstem connects above to the diencephalon by the transverse fissure of Bichat', but in standard teaching the transverse cerebral fissure (of Bichat) is a cleft separating the cerebral hemispheres from the diencephalon and brainstem; it does not join the midbrain to the diencephalon, which are directly continuous. A fissure is also not a connecting structure, and the packet's own question says it 'separates'. Not reported under conflicts.

summary: Cricothyroidotomy: A high-yield point and the subject of its own 'deeper' heading (emergency airway through the cricothyroid membrane); no concept or definition in the result mentions it. Likely a consequence of the limit.

External laryngeal nerve injury: Lesion of the external laryngeal nerve that paralyses the cricothyroid muscle, giving weakness of phonation from loss of its tightening effect on the vocal cords. The voice change is especially noticeable in singers.

evidence.quote: External laryngeal nerve: weakness of phonation from loss of the tightening effect of the cricothyroid

summary: Rima glottidis: A question asks directly what it is (the opening between the cords). The result has no concept for it and only lists it as an alias of the glottis compartment. A choice by the worker rather than a pure consequence of the 50-concept limit.

The packet says the medial eminence marks the midline of the floor of the fourth ventricle (one question option calls it the 'median eminence'). In standard teaching the midline is marked by the median sulcus, with a medial eminence on each side of it; 'median eminence' is the standard name of a hypothalamic structure.
detail: differs-from-standard-teaching

evidence.quote: The medial eminence marks the midline of the floor.
The median eminence marks the midline.

evidence.quote: If both recurrent and external laryngeal nerves are damaged on both sides, all the intrinsic muscles are paralysed and the cords are further abducted and fixed: the cadaveric position
Bilateral with external nerve: cadaveric position

summary: Glottis: wrong-alias
detail: 'Rima glottidis' is the standard name of a different, narrower thing: the opening between the vocal cords, which is how the packet's own question defines it. The concept is defined as the compartment at the level of the vocal cords, and the result makes the vocal fold part-of it, so it is not the gap. The packet's loose use should have gone under conflicts, not aliases.
